rationale: B wins by giving the founder four genuinely different desks without losing the plot: ownership, accountability, materials, and runner experience. A is cleaner on the facts, but its third angle, "Can a profitable public company make money renting out a shoe it grinds up?", leans hard on economics the update explicitly does not disclose. B's "The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" is softer than it should be, but it opens a real supply-chain lane A never finds.
gaps_in_A: "putting a core product behind" overstates the update; Cyclon is a running shoe, but the facts do not say it is a core product for On.
"Can a profitable public company make money renting out a shoe it grinds up?" is viable, but it is underfed by the provided facts because both the monthly fee and per-unit economics are missing.
A misses the runner/user lens entirely, even though the no-ownership model creates an obvious gear-review/customer-experience story.
The next step says "draft a tight pitch" before resolving monthly fee and recycling-rate gaps; that is too eager for angles the set itself admits are not yet pitchable.
gaps_in_B: "The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" implies a broader trend from a single On fact; it needs supply-chain evidence before that headline is safe.
"runners track shoe mileage obsessively" is plausible beat knowledge, but it is not in the update and should be framed as reporter-tested context, not a supplied fact.
"this model hands the retirement decision to the brand" may be true, but the return trigger is not disclosed; the set catches this later, but the angle headline/body gets ahead of the evidence.
The contrarian angle bundles "per-unit economics" into a circularity disclosure gap; useful, but recycling rate and unit economics are different accountability questions and should not be blurred.
